title: 1 Kings 2:1–12
context: The days of David draw near that he should die, and he commands Solomon his son. He is going “the way of all the earth.” Solomon is to be strong, to show himself a man, and to keep the instruction of the LORD his God, walking in his ways and keeping his statutes, commandments, ordinances, and testimonies, according to what is written in the law of Moses, that he may prosper, and that the LORD may establish the word spoken concerning David: “If your children are careful of their way, to walk before me in truth with all their heart and with all their soul, there shall not fail you,” he said, “a man on the throne of Israel.” David then turns to unfinished cases. Joab killed Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, shedding the blood of war in peace; Solomon is to act according to his wisdom and not let Joab’s gray head go down to Sheol in peace. The sons of Barzillai the Gileadite are to be shown kindness and to eat at Solomon’s table, as they came to David when he fled from Absalom. Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite of Bahurim, cursed David on the way to Mahanaim, later met him at the Jordan, and received David’s oath, “I will not put you to death with the sword.” David now tells Solomon not to hold him guiltless, and to bring his gray head down to Sheol with blood. David then sleeps with his fathers and is buried in David’s city. He reigned forty years, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. Solomon sits on his father’s throne, and his kingdom is firmly established. Readers in both traditions have evaluated the charges about Joab and Shimei in more than one way: some hear a just settlement of bloodguilt and a charge that leaves the manner of judgment to Solomon’s wisdom, even while David himself keeps the oath not to put Shimei to death with the sword; others find the instructions, especially about Shimei, hard or politically driven. That difference of evaluation runs inside both traditions and should not be turned into an Arminian–Reformed fork over the ethics of royal succession. The charge to keep the law, and concern for the LORD’s word about the throne, remain shared ground.

verses.text: Now the days of David came near that he should die; and he commanded Solomon his son, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now the days of David came near that he should die; and he commanded Solomon his son, saying,” The sentence opens a speech that runs through the next verses. David’s death is near, and the first act of the chapter is a charge to Solomon.

Arminian readers hear a father still responsible in his last days. He does not leave the kingdom without a word; he commands his son.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the opening as the start of a last charge, not as a sudden vacancy already filled by chance. The days came near, and David spoke.

Both traditions read the verse as the setting for what follows: a dying king addressing the son now seated after him.

verses.text: “I am going the way of all the earth. You be strong therefore, and show yourself a man;
verses.arminianNotes:
The speech begins, “I am going the way of all the earth. You be strong therefore, and show yourself a man;” The line continues into verse 3. Death is named as the way of all the earth, and Solomon is called to strength and to maturity in office.

Arminian readers hear a real exhortation. Solomon must himself be strong and show himself a man; the charge addresses his will and his conduct, not a path already walked for him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the common mortality David names and from the call that follows. “You be strong therefore, and show yourself a man” is spoken to the new king as his duty.

Both traditions take the opening of the charge as shared counsel. The particular cases later in the speech should not be read back into this first sentence as a party argument.

verses.text: and keep the instruction of the LORD your God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, his commandments, his ordinances, and his testimonies, according to that which is written in the law of Moses, that you may prosper in all that you do and wherever you turn yourself.
verses.arminianNotes:
The charge continues: Solomon is to “keep the instruction of the LORD your God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, his commandments, his ordinances, and his testimonies, according to that which is written in the law of Moses,” that he may prosper in all he does and wherever he turns.

Arminian readers hear a genuine condition of faithfulness. Prosperity is tied to keeping what is written in the law of Moses, a path Solomon must actually walk.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the standard is “the instruction of the LORD your God” and the law of Moses, not court custom alone. The new king is to walk in the LORD’s ways.

Both traditions take this as shared ground: the throne is not excused from the written law, and Solomon is called to keep it.

verses.text: Then the LORD may establish his word which he spoke concerning me, saying, ‘If your children are careful of their way, to walk before me in truth with all their heart and with all their soul, there shall not fail you,’ he said, ‘a man on the throne of Israel.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The purpose is then named: “Then the LORD may establish his word which he spoke concerning me,” saying, “If your children are careful of their way, to walk before me in truth with all their heart and with all their soul, there shall not fail you,” he said, “a man on the throne of Israel.” The word about the throne is recalled with an “If”.

Arminian readers hear that “If” as a real condition. The LORD’s word is sure, and the children’s careful walk in truth is not treated as a form of words without meaning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to erase the condition. The LORD’s word concerning David includes this call to walk before him in truth with all the heart and soul, and the continuing man on the throne is spoken of in that light.

Both traditions can confess the LORD’s faithfulness to his word here without making the verse a sovereignty fork. The charge is that Solomon and his children be careful of their way.

verses.text: “Moreover you know also what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, even what he did to the two captains of the armies of Israel, to Abner the son of Ner and to Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, and shed the blood of war in peace, and put the blood of war on his sash that was around his waist and in his sandals that were on his feet.
verses.arminianNotes:
David turns to Joab: “you know also what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, even what he did to the two captains of the armies of Israel, to Abner the son of Ner and to Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, and shed the blood of war in peace,” putting that blood on his sash and on his sandals. The speech continues into verse 6.

Arminian readers take the charge as a naming of bloodguilt already known. Joab’s killings in peacetime are not recast here; they are recalled as something Solomon knows.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the facts as David states them. Abner and Amasa, captains of Israel’s armies, were killed, and the blood of war was shed in peace.

Both traditions describe the accusation as the narrator, through David, gives it. How Solomon should answer it is taken up in the next verse, and later evaluations of that answer differ inside both traditions.

verses.text: Do therefore according to your wisdom, and don’t let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace.
verses.arminianNotes:
David says, “Do therefore according to your wisdom, and don’t let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace.” Solomon is to use wisdom, and Joab is not to go down to Sheol, the place here named for the dead, in peace.

Arminian readers hear a charge that still requires Solomon’s judgment. The phrase “according to your wisdom” leaves the manner with him, even as the end David names is not peace for Joab.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note both parts of the sentence: wisdom, and no peaceful descent to Sheol. The verse is a charge, not yet the act itself.

Readers in both traditions have judged this instruction in more than one way, some as a just refusal to leave bloodguilt unpaid, others as a hard word. That spread of evaluation is not an Arminian–Reformed fork, and it should not be forced into one.

verses.text: But show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table; for so they came to me when I fled from Absalom your brother.
verses.arminianNotes:
By contrast, Solomon is to “show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table; for so they came to me when I fled from Absalom your brother.” Kindness and a place at the table answer their earlier help.

Arminian readers hear a real debt of gratitude. The charge is not only about enemies; it is also about keeping faith with those who came to David in flight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same memory. Barzillai’s sons are to eat at the king’s table because their house came to David when he fled from Absalom.

Both traditions take the verse as a charge to kindness, set beside the harder cases, and they do not turn the table into a type.

verses.text: “Behold, there is with you Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite of Bahurim, who cursed me with a grievous curse in the day when I went to Mahanaim; but he came down to meet me at the Jordan, and I swore to him by the LORD, saying, ‘I will not put you to death with the sword.’
verses.arminianNotes:
David then names “Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite of Bahurim, who cursed me with a grievous curse in the day when I went to Mahanaim;” but who later came down to the Jordan, where David swore, “I will not put you to death with the sword.” The speech continues in verse 9. This Shimei is identified by father, tribe, and town; he should not be merged without care with the Shimei listed among David’s loyal men in 1:8.

Arminian readers hear both the curse and the oath. David himself did not put Shimei to death, and he says so.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the oath in view: “I will not put you to death with the sword.” The next verse will say what Solomon is to do; this verse first recalls what David swore.

Both traditions take the history as given, including the oath at the Jordan, before they consider the instruction that follows.

verses.text: Now therefore don’t hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man; and you will know what you ought to do to him, and you shall bring his gray head down to Sheol with blood.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now therefore don’t hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man; and you will know what you ought to do to him, and you shall bring his gray head down to Sheol with blood.” Solomon is again called wise, and the end named is a descent to Sheol with blood, not peace.

Arminian readers hear the tension the wording itself creates. David had sworn not to put Shimei to death with the sword; he now tells Solomon not to hold him guiltless and to bring his gray head down to Sheol with blood. The verse should be allowed to stand in that tension.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse a quick smoothing. Wisdom is again left with Solomon, and the charge is plain, even as David’s own oath remains in the previous verse.

Within both traditions, some hear a way of honoring David’s oath while leaving judgment to his successor, and others find the instruction hard or politically driven. That is an in-house difference of evaluation, not a party fork over royal succession, and it should be named as such.

verses.text: David slept with his fathers, and was buried in David’s city.
verses.arminianNotes:
“David slept with his fathers, and was buried in David’s city.” The charge has ended. The king dies, and he is buried in the city that bears his name.

Arminian readers hear a plain death. The way of all the earth, named in verse 2, is now walked, and the burial is reported without adornment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the verse as the narrator’s close of David’s life in this book. He slept with his fathers; he was buried in David’s city.

Both traditions receive the notice as shared history. The following verses will sum the reign and turn to Solomon’s seat.

verses.text: The days that David reigned over Israel were forty years; he reigned seven years in Hebron, and he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The days that David reigned over Israel were forty years; he reigned seven years in Hebron, and he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.” The narrator gives the official length of the reign, divided between Hebron and Jerusalem.

Arminian readers take the figures as the book’s own summary, matching the division already told in Samuel, without using them to settle later chronological debates the verse does not raise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let the numbers stand as given: forty years in all, seven in Hebron, thirty-three in Jerusalem.

Both traditions read the verse as a reign closed and counted, shared ground before the next king is seated in the following line.

verses.text: Solomon sat on David his father’s throne; and his kingdom was firmly established.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Solomon sat on David his father’s throne; and his kingdom was firmly established.” The unit ends with Solomon on the throne and the kingdom described as firmly established. Later in the chapter the narrator will say again, after further events, that the kingdom was established in Solomon’s hand.

Arminian readers hear a real seating and a real establishing already under way at David’s death, without denying that more remains to be told.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the verse as the narrator’s present assessment. The throne is David’s father’s throne, and the kingdom is firmly established.

Both traditions close the charge-and-death unit there, and they do not turn this establishing into a debate about succession ethics.
